html:
The settling of Iceland by Norse people between about 870 and 930. By tradition the first permanent settler was Ingólfr Arnarson, who built his farm at Reykjavík in 874.

The island was empty, except perhaps for a few Irish hermits. Most settlers came from western Norway, many by way of the Norse colonies in Scotland and Ireland, part of the wider Viking world. They brought Gaelic wives and slaves: DNA studies show that a large share of the first women were of Gaelic descent. The Book of Settlements names hundreds of the first settlers and their farms.

The settlers cut down the birch woods for farms and pasture, which led to soil loss still visible today. In 930 they set up the Althing, an open-air assembly and one of the oldest parliaments. Iceland became a commonwealth without a king, accepted Christianity in 1000, and produced the sagas. From Iceland, Norse sailors went on to Greenland and North America.
